text: Northbridge's catalog frontend is a React app, bundled down to static files. Everything before that only matters during the build. Shipping it all anyway bloats the image with tools the running container never touches. Multi-stage builds solve exactly this.

A single-stage build works, but the final image carries the full Node base, every dev dependency, the compiler, and the unbuilt source -- none of which the running app needs once the static output exists. That's hundreds of megabytes of tooling riding along with a handful of files.

FROM node 20 AS build names the first stage build. It has the full Node toolchain, installs dependencies from package.json, copies in the rest of the source, and runs the build, producing app slash dist -- a folder of plain HTML, JavaScript, and CSS.

The second FROM starts a completely fresh image, based on a minimal nginx instead of node at all. COPY dash dash from equals build reaches back into the build stage and copies out only the compiled output -- nothing else from that stage, not node_modules, not the compiler, not the source, makes it into the final image.

The result: forty-eight megabytes, versus what would easily be nine hundred or more with the full Node toolchain included. The build stage still ran npm install and the build command -- its weight just never carries into what ships.
That's multi-stage builds. Next up: more ways to keep an image lean -- slim bases, dockerignore, and minimizing layers.
